definition: Grammatical Framework (GF) is a programming language for writing grammars of natural languages.
details: GF is capable of parsing and generating texts in several languages simultaneously while working from a language-independent representation of meaning. Grammars written in GF can be compiled into a platform independent format and then used from different programming languages including C and Java, C#, Python and Haskell. A companion to GF is the GF Resource Grammar Library, a reusable library for dealing with the morphology and syntax of a growing number of natural languages. Both GF itself and the GF Resource Grammar Library are open-source. Typologically, GF is a functional programming language. Mathematically, it is a type-theoretic formal system (a logical framework to be precise) based on Martin-Löf's intuitionistic type theory, with additional judgments tailored specifically to the domain of linguistics.

explainer.lead: Grammatical Framework, or GF, is an open-source programming language for describing how natural languages work. It lets developers connect several languages to one shared representation of meaning, so the same grammar-based system can both understand and produce text.

tiers.eli5: Imagine writing one idea on a card, then giving the card to friends who each know a different language. GF works a bit like that: the idea stays the same, while separate grammar rules turn it into words for each language. It can also run backwards, taking a sentence apart to recover the idea on the card.
tiers.practitioner: An engineer defines an abstract syntax for meanings and concrete grammars that map those meanings into particular languages. GF grammars can be compiled into a platform-independent format and used from C, Java, C#, Python, or Haskell, with the Resource Grammar Library supplying reusable morphology and syntax. This is grammar engineering rather than model training: adding or improving language support requires suitable grammatical rules.
tiers.paperLevel: GF is a functional programming language and a type-theoretic logical framework based on Martin-Löf's intuitionistic type theory, extended with judgments specific to linguistics. In schematic terms, an abstract representation A is shared across languages, while each concrete grammar C_L supports generation A -> C_L and parsing C_L -> A. Its multilingual reach depends on the available concrete grammars and resource-library coverage.

explainer.example: An application can represent the meaning 'the cat sleeps' once, then use an English concrete grammar to generate "The cat sleeps" and a Swedish one to generate "Katten sover." The same mappings can be used in reverse to parse either sentence back into the shared meaning.

explainer.intuition: Separate what a sentence means from how a particular language expresses it. One abstract grammar captures the meaning, while concrete grammars supply each language's words and grammatical forms.
howItWorks: Define language-independent meanings in an abstract grammar.
Write concrete grammars that express those meanings in individual natural languages.
Reuse morphology and syntax from the GF Resource Grammar Library where available.
Compile the grammars into a platform-independent format for parsing or generation.
Call the compiled grammar from a host application in a supported programming language.
explainer.whyItMatters: GF keeps multilingual parsing and generation consistent by tying every supported language to the same meaning representation. Its reusable library and open-source implementation also reduce the need to rebuild basic grammatical machinery for each application.
misconceptions: GF is not a learned machine-translation model; it follows explicitly written grammars.
A shared meaning representation does not eliminate the need for language-specific grammar rules.
The Resource Grammar Library is a companion library for GF, not a separate programming language.
